title: the crossing of the Yamuna
hook: the guards fall asleep, the bolted doors swing open, and Vasudeva walks out into a storm carrying a newborn

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birth: four arms at midnight, and then, at Devaki's request, an ordinary baby on the prison floor. Your line was he becomes small enough to hold.

The baby has only just been born, and he cannot stay. Kamsa's guards are just outside. Prompted by the Lord himself, the Bhagavata says, Vasudeva picks up his son, and the prison starts to come undone. The guards slump into sleep. The doors, bolted and barred with iron, open on their own, the way darkness gives way to the sun. Outside, rain is falling and the clouds rumble low. Somewhere ahead, in the dark, is the river.
screen: `A NEWBORN SON.` → `THE GUARDS SLEEP.` → `THE DOORS OPEN BY THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Notice who does what. The miracles open the way, but they don't carry the child. Vasudeva does that, in his own arms, through a storm, at night. The Bhagavata adds two details. First, the rain. Shesha, the great serpent on whom Vishnu rests, follows behind Vasudeva and spreads his hoods over father and child like an umbrella. The cosmic serpent, holding off the weather for a newborn. Then the river. The Yamuna that night is swollen and fast, full of waves, whirlpools and foam, deep enough to stop anyone. And the river makes way, the text says, as the ocean once gave way for Rama when he crossed to Lanka to bring back Sita. The same Lord, another age, another stretch of water opening. Later retellings add more: in some, Vasudeva carries the baby in a basket on his head; in some, the river rises to touch the child's feet before it parts. The Bhagavata's own account is shorter: the father, the child, the serpent, the river giving way. Look back over this week and the same shape keeps returning. Yudhishthira refusing to leave a dog. Yudhishthira staying in the dark with his family. Vasudeva keeping a terrible promise. Now Vasudeva, walking into a flood with a baby. Help arrives in this week's stories, but someone still has to walk.
screen: `THE FATHER CARRIES THE CHILD` · `SHESHA SPREADS HIS HOODS` · `THE RIVER GIVES WAY` · then, large: `SOMEONE STILL HAS TO WALK`

segments.voice: Feel your feet rest flat on the floor; Vasudeva crossed on foot. Breathe in and bring to mind something you are carrying for someone else; breathe out and notice what has been holding off the rain for you: a friend, a habit, a faith, a bit of luck. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own way.
Shesha. The great serpent on whom Vishnu rests, who spreads his hoods over Vasudeva and the newborn child in the storm.
Your line: the river gives way. That's the week: a dog, a dark place, a promise, a river. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The crossing of the Yamuna is retold at Janmashtami in songs, plays and temple tableaux, and the image of Vasudeva carrying the infant through the river under Shesha's hoods is a familiar one in Hindu art.

gives way, as the ocean did for Rama

myth: in the Bhagavata, the river rises to touch the baby's feet
that comes from later retellings; the Bhagavata simply says the river gave way.
Shesha shelters the father and child from the rain
the serpent follows and spreads his hoods over them.

the bolted doors open on their own.

fork.setup: you're Vasudeva. the doors are open, it's pouring, and the river ahead is in flood. what do you do?
options: wait in the prison for the storm to pass.
walk out into the storm with the baby.
hide the baby somewhere in the city.
fork.reveal: he walks out at once, and Shesha shelters him while the Yamuna makes way.

original.note: shesha: the great serpent on whom Vishnu rests, who shelters the child in the storm.

trapdoor: what you thought: the river miraculously carried the baby across.
what it means: the river makes way, but Vasudeva carries his son himself, on foot, through the storm.
what a scholar hears: the Bhagavata compares the river to the ocean giving way for Rama, tying this night to another of Vishnu's descents.
guess: the great serpent Vishnu rests on, sheltering the child
the river goddess who parts the Yamuna's flood
the serpent who guards the doors of Kamsa's jail

chat.says: Did the river part all by itself, or did Vasudeva still have to walk?
options: The way opened, but Vasudeva still carried his son through the storm himself.
The river parted, and Shesha carried the baby across on his hoods.
Vasudeva waited on the bank until the flood dried up by morning.
chat.meaning: Miracles opened the doors and parted the river, but Vasudeva carried the child in his own arms.

Shesha.meaning: the great serpent on whom Vishnu rests

Vishnu.meaning: the great god who rests on the serpent Shesha

Yamuna.meaning: the river Vasudeva crosses to reach Gokula

Lanka.meaning: the island kingdom where Sita was held

Sita.meaning: Rama's wife, brought back from Lanka
